Foundations · Chapter 01 of 28

01 Purpose

Learn what Oath & Action does, and how its pillars and nonpartisan rules shape every piece.

Oath & Action is a nonpartisan publication and a set of tools for people in every state who live under public rules they rarely get to read. Our mission is “Help people understand and improve the rules that shape their lives.”

The ampersand in our name is the hinge, the joint a door swings on. It joins a promise to the action that keeps it, so every piece explains and tracks a decision, then turns to the people who make it and the step a reader can take. Chapter 04 draws the hinge and sets its rules.

In this chapter

  • Rule 01.1 Red never marks a party, a side or a person.
  • Rule 01.2 Two sides take Charcoal and Stone, with their names printed.
  • Rule 01.3 A diverging scale runs from Prussian through the page color to Verdigris.
  • Rule 01.4 On Prussian, identity marks turn White and data marks turn Newsprint.
  • Rule 01.5 Maps show a rule or a measure, never which party won a place.
  • Rule 01.6 Domes, columns and flags appear only in a captioned photograph of that place.
  • Rule 01.7 Brand graphics carry no party symbols, candidate photos, campaign gear or protest slogans.
  • Rule 01.8 Photographs show people doing public work, with who, what, where and when in the caption.
  • Rule 01.9 No atlas domain supplies more than one example in four, and no state more than one in five.
  • Rule 01.10 Examples rotate across levels of government and regions.
  • Rule 01.11 When majorities of both parties use a mechanism, show a case from each.
  • Rule 01.12 A rotation log records each example’s domain, state, level and backing coalition.
  • Rule 01.13 Name the office that decides, and name a party only when party is the mechanism.
  • Rule 01.14 Ask questions a supporter of the current rule could ask too.
  • Rule 01.15 Use plain verbs in place of war and sports metaphors.
  • Rule 01.16 Show both readings of a contested claim at the same length.
  • Rule 01.17 Describe a rule so its supporters would accept the description.
  • Rule 01.18 Both halves of a hinge pair share one color and weight, and only the ampersand is red.
  • Rule 01.19 People pairs join people through a shared rule or place, and their order rotates.
  • Rule 01.20 Party names, “left” and “right” enter a hinge headline only to report sourced agreement.
  • Rule 01.21 Every piece carries one content label in its kicker.
  • Rule 01.22 A process piece names the step and leaves the side to the reader.
  • Rule 01.23 A position piece wears its label before the headline and its fairness kit before the ask.
  • Rule 01.24 Name each product for what it does, and keep the ampersand for Oath & Action.

Rule 01.1 Red never marks a party, a side or a person.

Pillar Red never stands for a party, one side of a debate or a named person, in a chart, a map, a label or a headline. Each view gives its one working red to the job Rule 05.3 names, and none of those jobs is a side.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-data-emphasis-on-newsprint#121212
  • --oa-color-data-context-on-newsprint#5D636D
  • --oa-color-action-ask-fill-on-newsprint#E63946

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Election-night maps have taught readers to see red as one party. A red mark on a side tells a reader on the other side that the piece is against them before they read a word, and they stop trusting the record we keep for everyone.

Specifications

Working red
One job per view, in the order Rule 05.3 sets
--oa-color-action-ask-fill-on-newsprint
Sides of a vote
Charcoal and Stone, counts printed
--oa-color-data-context-on-newsprint

For builders

Rule 01.2 Two sides take Charcoal and Stone, with their names printed.

When a chart or table compares two parties or two sides, draw one in Charcoal and the other in Stone, or one solid and one in outline, and print each side’s name on its mark. Red never stands against blue or Verdigris.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-data-emphasis-on-newsprint#121212
  • --oa-color-data-context-on-newsprint#5D636D

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Red against blue reads as an election before it reads as data, and red against Verdigris stages the same contest in other hues. Neutral inks with printed names let a reader see who is who without learning a color code, and they hold in grayscale.

Specifications

First side
Charcoal, solid
--oa-color-data-emphasis-on-newsprint
Second side
Stone, solid, or a Charcoal outline
--oa-color-data-context-on-newsprint
Names
Printed on or beside each mark, in the text ink

Related chapters

  • 05 Color
  • 14 Data visualization later stage

For builders

Pick the data emphasis and data context tokens for the two sides, never a palette color by name, and set each side’s name as a direct label.

Rule 01.3 A diverging scale runs from Prussian through the page color to Verdigris.

A scale that shows change in two directions runs from Prussian through Newsprint to Verdigris. A boxed arrow and a word name each step’s direction, because the two hues lose their order in grayscale. Red and blue never form a diverging pair.

Tokens

  • --oa-chart-color-diverging-fill-step1-on-newsprint#1F2D5A
  • --oa-chart-color-diverging-fill-step2-on-newsprint#8E94A4
  • --oa-chart-color-diverging-fill-step3-on-newsprint#CECDC7
  • --oa-chart-color-diverging-fill-step4-on-newsprint#9AAEA6
  • --oa-chart-color-diverging-fill-step5-on-newsprint#3C5F59

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Neither end of the pair belongs to a party, so a fall and a rise carry the same weight. The arrow and the word carry the direction for a reader who sees no color at all.

Specifications

Steps
Five, step 1 the strongest fall, step 3 the page color
--oa-chart-color-diverging-fill-step3-on-newsprint
Direction
A boxed arrow in each step’s label ink, and a word

Rule 01.4 On Prussian, identity marks turn White and data marks turn Newsprint.

On a Prussian ground, set every identity mark in one color, White, the ampersand included. Draw data graphics on Prussian in Newsprint. Red never sits on Prussian.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-identity-signature-on-prussian#FFFFFF
  • --oa-color-data-emphasis-on-prussian#DCD9D2

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast

Pillar Red measures 3.19 to 1 against Prussian. At 16 px, where smoothing thins the strokes, the red ampersand measures 2.27 to 1 and a White one 8.27 to 1, so only White stays legible.

Specifications

Identity marks
White, one color
--oa-color-identity-signature-on-prussian
Data marks
Newsprint
--oa-color-data-emphasis-on-prussian

Rule 01.5 Maps show a rule or a measure, never which party won a place.

Color a map by the rule, count or measure the story is about, never by which party won each place. Use the neutral palette or a pattern, and set the key beside the map.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-data-emphasis-on-newsprint#121212
  • --oa-color-border-strong-on-newsprint#121212

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A map colored by winner splits the country into two camps and gives large, thinly settled states the most ink, when what a reader wants to know is whether a rule reaches the place where they live.

Specifications

Tile grid
12 columns by 8 rows, one square per state and DC

Charcoal, a Charcoal hatch and open, keyed in words

Rule 01.6 Domes, columns and flags appear only in a captioned photograph of that place.

Show a capitol dome, columns or a flag only inside a documentary photograph of that place or event, with a caption that names it. Keep them out of icons, backgrounds and textures.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Campaigns in both parties use the dome and the flag as shorthand for government. As decoration they stand for no rule, office or event, so they give the reader nothing to check or act on.

Related chapters

  • 16 Photography, illustration and video later stage
  • 12 Graphic devices and patterns later stage

For builders

Build cards from type and the brand’s own devices. A dome, a column or a flag enters only with a documentary photograph, its caption and its credit.

Rule 01.7 Brand graphics carry no party symbols, candidate photos, campaign gear or protest slogans.

Keep party symbols, candidate photographs, campaign merchandise and legible protest slogans out of brand graphics, since each takes a side the piece never argued. A party’s logo may appear as evidence, inside a sourced document the piece reproduces.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A reader takes any symbol on our page as ours. A campaign button or a slogan placard reads as an endorsement, even when the story beside it is neutral.

Related chapters

  • 16 Photography, illustration and video later stage
  • 23 Social and video later stage

For builders

When a story needs a party’s logo or a campaign’s material, place the whole document as a sourced image with its credit, never the symbol by itself.

Rule 01.8 Photographs show people doing public work, with who, what, where and when in the caption.

Choose photographs of people of different ages, places and roles doing public work, officials among them. Every caption names who is shown, what they are doing, where and when.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A reader trusts a picture of a real hearing more than a picture of the idea of one, and a full caption lets them check it.

Related chapters

  • 16 Photography, illustration and video later stage

For builders

Write the caption’s four parts before a photograph goes in: who, what, where and when. Until the photography direction is settled, use a labeled placeholder.

Rule 01.9 No atlas domain supplies more than one example in four, and no state more than one in five.

Within a chapter, draw no more than one example in four from any one of the atlas’s ten domains, and no more than one in five from any one state. Massachusetts examples may appear on the same terms as any other state’s.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A run of examples from one subject or one state tells readers whose problems we care about. Rotation keeps a reader in Texas and a reader in Maine in view of the same chapter.

Related chapters

  • 13 Evidence and sourcing later stage

For builders

Count from the rotation log before a chapter goes to review, using the atlas’s ten domains by their full names.

Rule 01.10 Examples rotate across levels of government and regions.

Draw examples from federal, state, county or city, and school district decisions, and from every region of the country.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Most of the rules that reach a household are written below the federal level. A reader who only ever sees Congress learns that the decisions nearest to them are not worth following.

Related chapters

  • 13 Evidence and sourcing later stage
  • 21 The atlas later stage

For builders

Tag each row of the rotation log with its level, and look for an empty level before review.

Rule 01.11 When majorities of both parties use a mechanism, show a case from each.

When majorities of either party use the same mechanism, show a documented case from each, at the same length. The test case is Loop R4a, the map-drawing loop, which the atlas titles “Majorities draw maps that help them keep control.”

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A mechanism shown through one party’s case reads as a charge against that party. With a case from each side, the mechanism itself stands out, and that is the part a reader can change.

Related chapters

  • 15 Systems graphics later stage
  • 13 Evidence and sourcing later stage

For builders

Before a piece runs a mechanism, list the party of the majority in each of the atlas’s case records for that loop, and pick one case from each.

Rule 01.12 A rotation log records each example’s domain, state, level and backing coalition.

Log every example with its atlas domain, its state, its level of government and, for any reform shown, the coalition that usually backs it. The studio reviews the log at each gate.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A chapter can lean toward one topic or one side without anyone noticing. A log turns balance into counts anyone can check, including a reader who suspects a lean.

Related chapters

  • 13 Evidence and sourcing later stage
  • 28 Standards checklist later stage

For builders

Keep one log row per example in the chapter’s notes and count domains and states from it before review.

Rule 01.13 Name the office that decides, and name a party only when party is the mechanism.

Say which office or body makes the decision. Name a party only when party is part of how the decision works, such as a party-line vote, and give the count and its source.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A reader can call an office or testify before it, and at the next election they can vote its members out. A party’s name in place of an office gives them a team to blame and nobody to call.

Related chapters

  • 02 Voice
  • 13 Evidence and sourcing later stage

For builders

Search a draft for “politicians”, “Washington”, “lawmakers” and party names, and replace each with the office that holds the decision.

Rule 01.14 Ask questions a supporter of the current rule could ask too.

Leave grievance words out of headlines, questions and calls to act, such as “rigged”, “broken”, “crisis” and “the rule you are angry about”. Write each question so a person who supports the current rule could ask it too.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A question that assumes the reader is angry tells half our readers the piece is not for them, while a question about who decided and when it could change invites everyone in.

Related chapters

  • 02 Voice
  • 23 Social and video later stage

For builders

Search a draft for the words this rule lists, and read each question as someone who likes the current rule would.

Rule 01.15 Use plain verbs in place of war and sports metaphors.

Describe a public decision in the words for what happens, such as propose, debate, vote and pass. Leave out war and sports metaphors such as fight, battle, front and game plan.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A war or a game needs an enemy or a loser, and the people on the other side of a vote are our readers too. The verbs for what happens also tell a reader where the decision stands.

Related chapters

  • 02 Voice

For builders

Search a draft for fight, battle, front, war and game plan, and name the step in the process in its place.

Rule 01.16 Show both readings of a contested claim at the same length.

When credible studies disagree, give the two readings equal length and the same verbs and type, and name who holds each one.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Equal space is how a reader sees that the disagreement is real. A long reading beside a short dismissal tells them which side we prefer before they weigh either.

Related chapters

  • 13 Evidence and sourcing later stage
  • 14 Data visualization later stage

For builders

Set both readings in one two-column block with matching labels and count their words before you publish.

Rule 01.17 Describe a rule so its supporters would accept the description.

Read your description of a rule as someone who supports it would. If they would object to the words, rewrite the description until they would accept it, and save the argument for a labeled position piece.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Readers who back a rule are among the people we serve, and many are the officials a reader is asked to contact, so the description has to hold for them as well.

Related chapters

  • 13 Evidence and sourcing later stage
  • 02 Voice

For builders

Before review, read the description in the place of someone who supports the rule, and mark every word they would change.

Rule 01.18 Both halves of a hinge pair share one color and weight, and only the ampersand is red.

Set both noun phrases of a hinge headline in the same ink, face and weight. Only the ampersand takes red, as the view’s working red.

Tokens

  • --oa-font-family-display"Inter Tight", Arial, sans-serif
  • --oa-color-palette-pillar-red#E63946

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

When one half is red or heavier, the headline takes a side between a rule and its result. Equal halves leave the joining to the ampersand.

Specifications

Related chapters

For builders

Set the headline in Inter Tight ExtraBold and place ampersand B’s display master at the cap height in place of the font’s ampersand. Chapter 04 gives the sizes.

Rule 01.19 People pairs join people through a shared rule or place, and their order rotates.

When a hinge headline joins two people or groups, join them through a rule or a place they share. Swap their order from one piece to the next, so neither always comes first.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

The ampersand stands for common ground, and people stand on it through something they share. A fixed order would rank one group above the other.

Related chapters

  • 04 The Ampersand and the hinge
  • 02 Voice

For builders

Log the order of each people pair, and swap it the next time a piece joins the same two groups.

Rule 01.20 Party names, “left” and “right” enter a hinge headline only to report sourced agreement.

Use “left”, “right” or a party’s name in a hinge headline only to report a point where the sides agree, such as a bill with sponsors from both parties, and source the agreement in the deck.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A red ampersand between two sides would mark the sides themselves, against Rule 01.1. Reporting agreement is the one case where naming the sides helps a reader.

Related chapters

  • 04 The Ampersand and the hinge
  • 02 Voice

For builders

When a headline names the sides, link the deck’s source line to the vote, the sponsor list or the survey that shows the agreement.

Rule 01.21 Every piece carries one content label in its kicker.

Open the kicker, the short line above a headline, with one content label: Explainer, Tracker, Analysis, Report, Act · How to take part, or Our position. A series name may follow the label.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-action-primary-fill-on-newsprint#121212

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

The label tells a reader what kind of claim the piece makes before they read it, and whether we are reporting or arguing.

Related chapters

  • 13 Evidence and sourcing later stage
  • 09 Pillar marks later stage

For builders

Pick the label from the six in this rule. A piece that fits none of them needs a ruling before it runs.

Rule 01.22 A process piece names the step and leaves the side to the reader.

An Act piece labeled “Act · How to take part” gives one step with its date and place, sets out what supporters and opponents have said at the same length, and takes no side. Its ask is the view’s one working red.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-action-ask-fill-on-newsprint#E63946
  • --oa-color-action-ask-label-on-newsprint#FFFFFF
  • --oa-component-button-ask-keyline-on-newsprint#121212

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A reader of any view can use a process piece, because it tells them how to be heard and leaves what to say to them.

Kicker
Act · How to take part, in plain type
Ask
Pillar Red fill, White label at 19 px bold, Charcoal keyline on Newsprint

Before the ask

  • 12 Graphic devices and patterns later stage
  • 18 Components and interaction later stage

For builders

Build the ending from the hinge divider, the “What you can do” heading and one ask button. Link the neutral tracker, never a campaign page.

Rule 01.23 A position piece wears its label before the headline and its fairness kit before the ask.

A piece that asks readers to support or oppose a named measure opens its kicker with the label “Our position”, before the headline. Before the ask it gives the strongest case against the position, what we don’t know and a disclosure of who decided.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-action-primary-fill-on-newsprint#121212
  • --oa-color-action-ask-fill-on-newsprint#E63946

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A reader who disagrees with us can still trust the rest of our coverage when each argument carries its label and its strongest opposing case.

Specifications

Label first
“Our position” opens the kicker, before the headline, and a shared card keeps it top left.
The strongest case against
The opposing case as its supporters would put it, sourced, at least a third of the argument’s length.
Grades kept
Every claim keeps its evidence grade, and its verb matches the grade.
Opponents by role
Opponents are named by office or role, never by party as a villain.
What we don’t know
The open questions, named.
Process facts
Who decides, when and how, word for word as the neutral tracker gives them.
Disclosure
Who decided the position, the date and any funder interest, above the ask, with the public position log.
Never in the record
Positions never appear in the atlas, the trackers or the data.

Related chapters

  • 13 Evidence and sourcing later stage
  • 18 Components and interaction later stage

For builders

Use the position label component, never a plain kicker, and check the eight kit items in this rule’s specifications before the piece goes to the editor.

Rule 01.24 Name each product for what it does, and keep the ampersand for Oath & Action.

Give each product a plain name that says what it does, signed by Oath & Action. The atlas is the only product named as a question, and no product name holds an ampersand; a partner’s ampersand is written as “and”.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

One masterbrand means one trust mark, so a reader who trusts the newsletter can trust the tracker it links to. A plain name tells them what they will get before they open it.

Related chapters

  • 03 Identity
  • 22 Newsletter and email later stage

For builders

Name a new product as its subject plus its kind, such as “Child Care Rules Tracker”, and run the name past this rule and Rule 01.15 before it ships.

Foundations · Chapter 02 of 28

02 Voice

Write the way you’d explain a rule to a neighbor, and quote the brand lines exactly.

Our tagline is “A country that answers to its people.” People can hold an office to account once they know which office decided. So we name who acts, in words you would use at a kitchen table, as in “A regulator or a board approves your rate.”

Our reader promise is “We explain how a decision is made and give you a practical way to take part.” A reader can take part only in a decision they can follow, which is why clarity comes first in our editorial commitment, “Clarity is our duty. Action is our promise.”

Rule 02.1 W01 Write it the way you would say it.

Write the way you would explain something to a neighbor, in everyday words and full sentences. Read the draft aloud and rewrite any line you would not say.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

Most readers meet us on a phone, between other things. A sentence they can follow by ear the first time is the one they can act on.

Specifications

Group
1. Sound like a person talking
Before
Our brand guide, fifth edition, the sample research brief in its Reports chapter

Related chapters

For builders

Read the draft aloud, or have a screen reader read it to you, and rewrite each line where you stumble or stop to decode.

Rule 02.2 W02 Name who acts.

Put the person or office that acts in front of the verb. When you find a passive verb, ask who does the action and name them.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

People can hold an office to account only when they can name it. Putting the actor first gives them the name in the first breath.

For builders

Search for “is”, “are”, “was” and “were” before a past participle, and for “by”, and ask who does the action.

Rule 02.3 W03 Change the length of your sentences.

Mix short sentences with long ones, and keep the mix hard to predict. A run of sentences the same size starts to sound like a metronome.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

Speech rises and falls. When every sentence runs the same length, a listener starts to hear the beat over the words.

Specifications

Group
1. Sound like a person talking
Before
Our systems atlas, Who Do They Answer To?, reform profile “Rules for drug-pricing middlemen (PBMs)”, how it would be carried out

For builders

Count the words in each sentence of a paragraph. If every count falls within a few words of the others, join two sentences or split one.

Rule 02.4 W04 Join thoughts that belong together.

Use the small words that show how thoughts connect, such as because, so, when and once. Save short sentences for the moments that need one.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

Words such as because and once carry the logic a listener needs. Without them, the reader has to guess how one short sentence leads to the next.

Specifications

Group
1. Sound like a person talking
Before

For builders

Look for runs of short sentences with no joining word, and join the ones that depend on each other with because, so, when or once.

Rule 02.5 W05 Open with something the reader can use.

Make the first sentence give the reader a fact or a step. Cut lines that only announce what comes next, and stock phrases that lean on the words after them.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A reader decides in the first line whether a piece is worth their time, and a line that only announces what is coming gives them no reason to stay.

Rule 02.6 W06 Give the point without a reveal.

Put the point where the reader meets it first. A colon or a teaser sentence that holds it back for effect only makes the reader wait.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A reveal makes the reader wait for a point we could have given at once, and holding it back sounds like a performance.

Rule 02.7 W07 Stop when the facts stop.

End a paragraph on its last useful fact, and cut any line after it that only restates the point.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A closing line that restates the point tells the reader we doubt they followed, so we end on the last new fact and trust them with it.

Rule 02.8 W08 Close without a slogan.

End a piece or section on the last thing the reader needs, usually a step with its date. Where a sign-off line belongs, use the locked tagline.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

The last words of a piece are the ones a reader carries away. A dated step gives them something to do with what they read.

Rule 02.9 W09 Say what a thing is.

Tell the reader what something is. Leave out the turn that first says what it is not, and the phrases set against each other for effect.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A sentence that starts with what a thing is not makes the reader picture the wrong thing first and then undo it.

Rule 02.10 W10 Drop the matched pair.

Write the relation between two things as a plain sentence. Two short halves set side by side sound like a slogan and leave the reader to supply the link.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

Two matched halves sound like a slogan and leave the reader to supply the link between them, which one plain sentence can state.

Rule 02.11 W11 Skip the run of negatives.

When you rule several things out, put them in one list under one verb and give the reason.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A run of negatives sounds like a list of grievances. One verb and a reason tell the reader what to do and why.

Rule 02.12 W12 List what the facts hold.

Give a list as many items as the facts hold. When there are three, vary their shape so they do not fall into a chant.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

Three items in a row sound finished, so writers reach for three when the facts hold two or four. A list sized to the facts sounds like advice.

Rule 02.13 W13 Give each sentence its own shape.

Build each sentence in a paragraph on its own frame. When several in a row open the same way, combine them or recast one.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

When sentences in a row open the same way, a listener hears the pattern and stops hearing the content.

Rule 02.14 W14 Pull stacked nouns apart.

When three or more nouns pile up, pull them apart with a preposition or a verb, so a listener can find the main noun.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A listener holds each noun in a stack until the last one says what the phrase is about. Pulling the stack apart puts the main noun first.

Rule 02.15 W15 Use the verb inside the noun.

When a noun hides a verb, use the verb and name who does it.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A noun made from a verb hides who acts, and turning it back into the verb brings the actor back into the sentence.

Rule 02.16 W16 Drop the hedges and keep the grade.

State a claim at the strength its evidence holds. When the evidence grade calls for “may” or “can”, use that word once and cut the other softeners.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A stack of softeners blurs how sure we are, while one grade verb, taken from the atlas’s scale, tells the reader how far the evidence goes.

Rule 02.17 W17 Cut the intensifiers.

Cut words that try to add force, such as genuinely, really, truly, actually, simply and just. If the sentence feels weak without one, give it a stronger fact.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A word added for force signals that the sentence is missing a fact, and the fact, once found, carries the force by itself.

Rule 02.18 W18 Use everyday verbs.

Pick the word you would say out loud. Write “use” for leverage, and “show” for underscore or reflect.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

Memo verbs put distance between the writer and the reader, while the words a resident would use at a council meeting sound like a neighbor talking.

Rule 02.20 W20 Size each word to its evidence.

Give an adjective or a label no more weight than its evidence carries, and when we praise our own work, label the praise as a design judgment.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A word that claims more than the evidence invites a reader to check it and find it wrong, and one wrong word costs the trust the rest of the page earned.

Rule 02.21 W21 Leave out the em dash.

Where you want an em dash, end the sentence, or join the parts with a comma and a word such as “and” or “because”.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

Rule 02.22 Follow the 12 house rules on every page.

Every page follows the 12 house rules, from quoting the locked lines exactly to calling a contested policy by its neutral name. They apply to headings, labels, captions and chart keys as well as to sentences.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

These are details a reader relies on without noticing, such as a date written in words and a source line they can follow back to its table. Each one keeps a page easy to check and fair to every reader.

Rule 02.25 Publish the mechanism behind a mood.

Rule 02.26 Use the words a reader would use, and spell series names exactly.

Write rule, decision, record, hearing and vote, the words a reader uses for public business. Leave out the words this rule lists, define each term of art at first use, and spell the six series names exactly.

Foundations · Chapter 03 of 28

03 Identity

Pick the lockup that fits the surface and size, and give it room on every side.

The wordmark is our name drawn as one piece of artwork: OATH and ACTION in heavy capitals, joined by ampersand B, the red ampersand we drew for Oath & Action. A lockup is a fixed arrangement of the wordmark with another part, such as the tagline or the lockmark, the 3 by 3 grid of nodes that chapter 08 explains.

Every mark here is a vector master drawn for a range of sizes. You place the master, color it with tokens and leave room around it. In this chapter x means the height of the wordmark’s capitals, and the pages show today’s wordmark width; a condensed width appears only in the proofs for Gate 2 after chapter 08.

In this chapter

  • Rule 03.1 Place the wordmark from its master file.
  • Rule 03.2 Choose the lockup by the space and the surface.
  • Rule 03.3 Keep one cap height of clear space on every side.
  • Rule 03.4 Keep every mark at or above its minimum size.
  • Rule 03.5 Set the marks in their colors on the four approved surfaces.
  • Rule 03.6 Use L3 for the masthead, and drop the lockmark when the bar gets narrow.
  • Rule 03.7 Use L8 as the one monogram, and retire the spaced “O & A”.
  • Rule 03.8 Join a partner with a hairline, and keep our ampersand inside our name.

Rule 03.1 Place the wordmark from its master file.

Use the master drawn for the height you need and set its color with tokens. Never type the name in a font, Inter Tight included, though the capitals were cut from it.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

The masters set every gap between letters by eye and give the ampersand the same white on each side, 0.203x, so the name keeps one shape from a 16 px email footer to a printed banner. Ampersand B exists only as drawn artwork. A typed name takes the font’s ampersand and the font’s spacing, and a reader who meets two slightly different names starts to wonder which one is ours.

Rule 03.2 Choose the lockup by the space and the surface.

Eight lockups cover every use, and each has one job. Start from the width you have: L1 for most uses, L3 for the site and email masthead, L2 for square formats and posters, L8 where the full name will not fit. The table after this rule names all eight.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A fixed set means a reader meets the same arrangement in the same place, and a producer never has to invent one. Each lockup’s job comes from the space it fills, so the choice turns on two facts you can measure: the width you have and the surface under it.

Leave 1.0x of open space around the lockup’s outer edge, with its tagline and lockmark inside that edge. Text, rules, image edges and other logos all stay outside it. Over a photograph, set the lockup on a solid Newsprint or Charcoal panel with the same space inside the panel.

Rule 03.4 Keep every mark at or above its minimum size.

On screen, no identity mark draws its capitals under 14 px, and no tagline inside a lockup sets under 13 px. In print, no capitals under 3 mm and no tagline under 7 pt. Under a lockup’s minimum, switch to the lockup the table names.

Foundations · Chapter 04 of 28

04 The Ampersand and the hinge

Use the ampersand once per composition to join a commitment to what it produces.

The ampersand is the hinge of the brand. It joins an oath, the commitment a person or an office makes, to the action that keeps it, and in our headlines it joins a rule to its result. Ampersand B is our own drawing: one pen path that crosses itself at the waist, with a beak at the top right and a tail that lands on the baseline.

This chapter covers B drawn alone and the four places the hinge appears: the hinge headline, the hinge divider, the hinge diagram and the hinge-circle badge. It ends with the tiles for avatars and the app icon, and the large crop for covers.

In this chapter

  • Rule 04.1 Draw the ampersand from B’s master for its size.
  • Rule 04.2 Give each composition one ampersand moment.
  • Rule 04.3 Join a rule to its result with a hinge headline, and give its ampersand the view’s working red.
  • Rule 04.4 Set a hinge divider between how a decision is made and what you can do about it.
  • Rule 04.5 Show the hinge diagram on its own, to explain the idea.
  • Rule 04.6 Use the hinge-circle badge only to close a piece, on a back cover or at events.
  • Rule 04.7 Put B on a Charcoal tile for avatars and the app icon.
  • Rule 04.8 Crop a large B off the bottom-right corner only.
  • Specifications
  • Related chapters

Rule 04.1 Draw the ampersand from B’s master for its size.

B has three masters: the 16 px master for 16 to 23 px tall, the 24 px master for 24 to 47 px, and the display master from 48 px. Place the one whose range holds your height. A narrow drawing of B serves the condensed wordmark alone.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-identity-signature-on-newsprint#E63946

Why it works

Basis Design judgment, measured in Chromium (Identity masters notes, October 28, 2026)

B’s strokes swell and thin at 1.74 to 1, so the glyph keeps its color beside the heavy capitals, and its waist crossing sits on the center line that the hinge diagram draws through its nodes. The small masters sit on the pixel grid: at 16 px, 66 percent of B’s ink pixels are solid, where Edition 05’s scaled glyph reached 48 percent.

Rule 04.2 Give each composition one ampersand moment.

A composition is one view: a screen, a card, a slide or a printed page. It carries one ampersand moment, a hinge headline, a freestanding B or a cropped B. The wordmark’s own ampersand and the hinge divider do not count.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

The ampersand carries the brand’s idea, and a reader takes in one hinge at a time. With two or three on a card, each says less and the eye has no place to land.

Rule 04.3 Join a rule to its result with a hinge headline, and give its ampersand the view’s working red.

A hinge headline joins two noun phrases with B, as in “The zoning code & the rent.” B takes the view’s working red, the one red each view may spend, unless an error or a step the reader can take now already holds it. Then B takes the headline’s ink.

The headline names a mechanism in five or six words, and the red ampersand marks the joint. Rule 05.3 ranks an error first and the step a reader can take now second, so on an Act piece with a red button the step keeps the red.

Rule 04.4 Set a hinge divider between how a decision is made and what you can do about it.

The hinge divider is a 1 px hairline broken by a small B, drawn whole in the surface’s ink: Charcoal on Newsprint and White, Newsprint on Charcoal, White on Prussian. It is never red.

Rule 04.5 Show the hinge diagram on its own, to explain the idea.

The hinge diagram draws OATH and ACTION on a line with four nodes, B in a ring between them, two solid arcs running clockwise, and UNDERSTAND and IMPACT beneath. Keep it out of any view that holds the wordmark or a figure with a key, and use the divider where a page needs a break.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-identity-signature-on-newsprint#E63946
  • --oa-color-graphic-subtle-on-newsprint#5D636D

Why it works

Basis Design judgment; the five separation rules approved with I6 (G1-01)

The diagram teaches the brand’s idea in one picture: a promise becomes action, and the result shapes the next promise. Its arcs are solid because Atlas V7 draws a hypothesis as a dotted line and a plausible link as a dashed one. It carries words alone, with no ID, sign, grade, delay or count, so no reader takes it for one of the atlas’s loops.

Rule 04.6 Use the hinge-circle badge only to close a piece, on a back cover or at events.

The badge is B inside the hinge diagram’s ring, with no words. It ends an article or a report and marks event materials. Keep it away from avatars and favicons, from candidates and ballots, and from any view with the wordmark or the hinge diagram, and add no words or dates to it.

A ring of words and a founding date turn a badge into a seal, and Edition 05 put the reason plainly: “Seals imply an authority we do not claim.” A wordless badge closes a piece the way a period closes a sentence.

Rule 04.8 Crop a large B off the bottom-right corner only.

On a cover or a section opener, a large B may run off the bottom-right corner with up to 40 percent of the glyph outside the frame. It takes the surface’s ink, stays clear of the text, and never enters the top-left corner where reading starts.

Foundations · Chapter 05 of 28

05 Color

Choose a surface first, then the text and graphic colors that pass on it.

Oath & Action works in seven colors, and each one has a job. Newsprint, a warm off-white, is the page most of our work sits on, and Charcoal carries the words. Pillar Red marks one thing in each view, while Prussian, Stone, Verdigris and White support the rest.

Every pair in this chapter carries a contrast ratio: how far apart two colors sit in lightness, from 1 to 1 for the same color up to 21 to 1 for black on white, by the formula in the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). We measured each ratio on the token values. Pick the surface, and the tables tell you which text and marks can sit on it.

In this chapter

  • Rule 05.2 Text sits only on color pairs that pass.
  • Rule 05.3 Each view carries one working red.
  • Rule 05.4 Every state shows a word or a shape as well as a color.
  • Rule 05.5 Marks that carry meaning pass 3 to 1, and red on Newsprint takes a Charcoal keyline.
  • Rule 05.6 A tint has one named job, and identity marks never use one.
  • Rule 05.7 Charts and the atlas sit on Newsprint and take the chart palette.

Rule 05.1 Newsprint covers most of every page.

Newsprint covers 60 to 85 percent of every view. A dark panel in Charcoal or Prussian marks a turn in the reading, so a section holds one at most, and Pillar Red stays within 5 percent. Across a body of work, the seven colors keep the shares in the palette sheet below this rule.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-palette-charcoal#121212

  • --oa-color-palette-verdigris#4A7C74
  • --oa-color-palette-white#FFFFFF

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A warm, light page keeps long reading calm, and readers come to know Newsprint as ours before they read a word. A dark panel works as a signal only while it stays rare: each one tells the reader the section has turned, for example from an explanation to the dates that follow from it.

Rule 05.2 Text sits only on color pairs that pass.

Text under 24 px, or under 18.66 px in bold, needs a contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1 against its surface. Larger text needs 3 to 1. Take the primary and secondary text tokens for the surface, and read any other pair’s ratio in the tables below. Never judge a pair by eye.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-text-primary-on-newsprint#121212
  • --oa-color-text-primary-on-white#121212
  • --oa-color-text-primary-on-charcoal#DCD9D2
  • --oa-color-text-primary-on-prussian#FFFFFF
  • --oa-color-text-secondary-on-newsprint#4E535B
  • --oa-color-text-secondary-on-white#4E535B
  • --oa-color-text-secondary-on-charcoal#A3A19C
  • --oa-color-text-secondary-on-prussian#A3A19C

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3

WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) sets 4.5 to 1 for text and 3 to 1 for large text, which it defines as 18 point, or 14 point bold: 24 px and 18.66 px on screen. Readers with low vision need that margin, and so does anyone reading a phone in sunlight.

Stone, the secondary text color in our fifth edition, measures 4.29 to 1 on Newsprint. Secondary text on light surfaces now takes Deep Stone, Stone mixed 18 percent toward Charcoal, at 5.49 to 1. On dark surfaces it takes Dim Newsprint.

For builders

Choose the surface, then the role: secondary text on Prussian is --oa-color-text-secondary-on-prussian. Inside a surface class, --oa-color-text-secondary resolves to the same value. A pair with no token is a pair we have not measured, so add a token under Rule 05.6 before you use it.

Rule 05.3 Each view carries one working red.

The wordmark’s ampersand and the lockmark’s lever are signature red and do not count, and neither do the ampersands inside the hinge diagram and the hinge-circle badge, which are identity marks. The hinge diagram never shares a view with the wordmark and never stands in for the hinge divider. An icon’s red accent counts as signature red when the icon stands alone, as an app tile, an avatar or a single feature icon. In a row or a menu, icons go one color and only the current one keeps its red, and that red counts as signature red. Each view (one screen, card, slide or printed page) then carries one working red, in this order of precedence: an error the reader must fix; the step a reader can take now; the one point the headline names, which in a systems figure is where a reform acts. One job may take several marks, such as each target of one reform. A hinge headline’s ampersand uses the view’s working red. The hinge divider’s ampersand takes its surface’s ink: Charcoal on Newsprint and White, Newsprint on Charcoal, White on Prussian. In the guide itself, specimens, labeled failure cases and palette swatches do not count. Red never sits on Prussian.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-identity-signature-on-newsprint#E63946
  • --oa-color-state-error-mark-on-newsprint#E63946

  • --oa-color-identity-hinge-divider-on-newsprint#121212

Why it works

Basis Design judgment; decisions D2-01 and DR-66

One red tells the eye where to go first. The order settles which mark gets it when two compete: a reader has to fix an error before taking a step, and a step a reader can take matters more than a point we want to make. Signature red is part of the marks themselves, so it never competes with the working red.

Red never sits on Prussian, where it measures 3.19 to 1 and reads as a party pair of red and blue. On Newsprint it measures 2.96 to 1, so a working red mark there takes a Charcoal keyline (Rule 05.5).

Rule 05.4 Every state shows a word or a shape as well as a color.

Each interface state, from hover to error, changes its text or its shape along with its color. A disabled control stays readable and says what will make it available. State colors are their own set, kept apart from identity color and from the chart palettes in chapter 14.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-focus-ring-on-newsprint#4A7C74

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1 and 1.4.11

WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.1 Use of Color asks that a state show something besides color, and 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast asks 3 to 1 for the edges and focus rings that show one. Pillar Red and Verdigris measure 1.14 to 1 against each other, so a red error and a Verdigris success look alike to many readers unless a word and a glyph differ too.

Rule 05.5 Marks that carry meaning pass 3 to 1, and red on Newsprint takes a Charcoal keyline.

An icon, a chart mark, a control’s edge or a focus ring needs a ratio of 3 to 1 against its surface. Pillar Red measures 2.96 to 1 on Newsprint, so a red mark that carries meaning there takes a 1 px Charcoal keyline. Stone passes for marks on light surfaces, and a hairline that carries no meaning may sit lower.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-graphic-essential-on-newsprint#121212
  • --oa-color-graphic-subtle-on-newsprint#5D636D

  • --oa-chart-color-point-keyline-on-newsprint#121212

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11

WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast asks 3 to 1 for the parts of a graphic a reader needs and for the edges of controls. The keyline gives a red mark an edge the eye can find, at 13.29 to 1, while the fill keeps its red. Stone context bars measure 4.29 to 1, so they pass without help.

Draw the keyline inside the shape, with box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px in HTML or a 1 px stroke on an inner path in SVG, so the mark keeps its size. On White and Charcoal, where red measures 4.17 and 4.49 to 1, a red mark needs no keyline.

Rule 05.6 A tint has one named job, and identity marks never use one.

A tint is one palette color mixed toward Newsprint or Charcoal by a recorded amount, for one job. It enters only as a token, with its measured ratio. The wordmark, the ampersand, the lockmark and the pillar marks stay in solid palette colors, and no color on a page comes from lowering opacity.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-derived-deep-stone#4E535B
  • --oa-color-derived-dim-newsprint#A3A19C
  • --oa-color-derived-error-band#E1C9C1
  • --oa-color-tint-stone-n70#B4B4B3
  • --oa-color-tint-prussian-n62#8E94A4
  • --oa-color-tint-verdigris-n55#9AAEA6

Why it works

Basis Design judgment; Master Brief section 10; decision D1-04

Our fifth edition said “There are no tints.” Charts, error messages and selected rows need lighter and darker steps that no palette color supplies, so Edition 06 allows tints that meet five conditions: a measured need, a recorded mix, one job, a passing ratio on every surface it serves and a registered token.

We mix in OKLab, a color space where equal steps look equal, which keeps a tint’s hue steady as it lightens. Opacity gives no such control: Charcoal at 40 percent on Newsprint measures 2.48 to 1, where the Deep Stone token measures 5.49.

For builders

Write a new tint as a recipe in the token source, never as a hex in a page: mix('stone', 'newsprint', 0.70). The generator computes the hex and every ratio, and the rule test fails a tint with no registered need. In CSS the same mix is color-mix(in oklab, var(--oa-color-palette-stone), var(--oa-color-palette-newsprint) 70%).

Rule 05.7 Charts and the atlas sit on Newsprint and take the chart palette.

Newsprint is the page color for charts and the atlas. The series a title names takes Charcoal, and every other series takes Stone. Values that rise and fall run from Prussian through the page color to Verdigris, with an arrow or a printed sign carrying the direction. A party takes the same neutral ink as every other party, with its name printed on the mark, and Pillar Red reaches data only as the view’s one working red.

Tokens

  • --oa-chart-color-subject-on-newsprint#121212
  • --oa-chart-color-context-on-newsprint#5D636D
  • --oa-chart-color-diverging-fill-step1-on-newsprint#1F2D5A
  • --oa-chart-color-diverging-fill-step5-on-newsprint#3C5F59
  • --oa-chart-color-sequential-fill-step5-on-newsprint#36544F
  • --oa-chart-color-party-mark-on-newsprint#121212
  • --oa-chart-color-point-on-newsprint#E63946

Why it works

Basis Design judgment; decisions DR-48, DR-53, DR-54 and DR-58

On Newsprint, a chart shared on its own still reads as ours. A scale from red to blue reads as a party split in the United States, which a nonpartisan publication has to avoid. Under each color-vision simulation we ran, the closest steps of Prussian to Verdigris stay at least 0.106 apart in OKLab, about 5 times the 0.02 that CSS Color 4 treats as the smallest visible difference. In grayscale both ends print dark, at 0.31 and 0.46 OKLab lightness against 0.85 at the midpoint, so without the arrow a reader cannot tell a rise from a fall.

Foundations · Chapter 06 of 28

06 Type

Set every word at a readable size with the three faces and the type scale.

Three typefaces carry every word we publish: Inter Tight for headlines and big figures, Inter for reading and the interface, and Lora Italic for the words we quote. Each has a single job, so a reader can tell a headline from a quotation before reading either.

We set sizes in rem, a unit tied to the reader’s own text setting, which is 16 px unless they change it. A reader who enlarges text gets larger type everywhere, and no text on screen sets below 13 px.

In this chapter

  • Rule 06.1 Each typeface keeps its one job.
  • Rule 06.2 Every size comes from the type scale.
  • Rule 06.3 No text on screen sets below 13 px.
  • Rule 06.4 Tracking tightens only as headings grow.
  • Rule 06.5 Figures line up in tables, and negatives take the true minus sign.
  • Rule 06.6 Headings balance their lines and never end on one word.
  • Rule 06.7 Opening quotation marks hang outside the text edge.
  • Rule 06.8 Body text runs 60 to 75 characters a line.
  • Rule 06.9 Email sets its type in the system stack.
  • Rule 06.10 Pages load the three faces and never substitute another.
  • Specifications
  • Related chapters
  • For builders

Rule 06.1 Each typeface keeps its one job.

Inter Tight 800 sets titles, headings and big figures. Inter sets body text, the interface, labels, captions, tables and chart text, at 400, 600 and 700. Lora Italic sets only quoted words, such as a pull quote or a quote card, at 400, or at 500 on a quote card.

Tokens

  • --oa-font-family-display"Inter Tight", Arial, sans-serif
  • --oa-font-family-readingInter, Arial, sans-serif
  • --oa-font-family-quoteLora, Georgia, serif
  • --oa-font-weight-extrabold800
  • --oa-font-weight-regular400
  • --oa-font-weight-semibold600
  • --oa-font-weight-bold700
  • --oa-font-weight-medium500

Why it works

Basis Design judgment; Master Brief section 3; decision DR-47

One face for each job lets a reader tell a headline from a quotation at a glance. The wordmark is drawn from Inter Tight 800, so our headings share its voice, and the page still reads as ours with the logo covered. Charts follow the same split: Inter Tight for titles, Inter for labels and numbers, and Lora Italic only for quoted words.

Load all three with one link: https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Inter:wght@400;600;700&amp;family=Inter+Tight:wght@800&amp;family=Lora:ital,wght@1,400;1,500&amp;display=swap. Then set faces only through --oa-font-family-display, --oa-font-family-reading and --oa-font-family-quote.

Rule 06.2 Every size comes from the type scale.

Set text in the fourteen styles of the scale, with no sizes between them. Display styles grow with the window from 390 to 1440 px wide, reading styles hold one size, and every size is in rem so it follows the reader’s text setting.

Tokens

  • --oa-type-titleInter Tight 800, 6.875rem/0.95
  • --oa-type-sectionInter Tight 800, 5rem/1.03
  • --oa-type-h3Inter Tight 800, 2rem/1.08
  • --oa-type-h4Inter Tight 800, 1.5rem/1.15
  • --oa-type-quoteLora 400, 2rem/1.3
  • --oa-type-introInter 400, 1.375rem/1.5
  • --oa-type-bodyInter 400, 1.0625rem/1.6
  • --oa-type-body-smallInter 400, 0.9375rem/1.6
  • --oa-type-uiInter 600, 0.9375rem/1.4
  • --oa-type-captionInter 400, 0.875rem/1.5
  • --oa-type-labelInter 700, 0.8125rem/1.4
  • --oa-type-data-labelInter 600, 0.8125rem/1.3
  • --oa-type-figureInter Tight 800, 6.5rem/1
  • --oa-type-askInter 700, 1.1875rem/1.2

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.4

WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.4 Resize Text asks that text grow to 200 percent with nothing lost. A size in rem grows when a reader raises the browser’s text size, and a size fixed in px stays where it is. Our fifth edition set every size in px, and when we doubled its root text size in a test, none of its 2,383 text elements grew.

For builders

Set a style with its shorthand and its parts: font: var(--oa-type-body) carries face, weight, size and line height, and letter-spacing, text-transform and font-variant-numeric each have their own property, such as --oa-type-label-letter-spacing. Never write a font size in px.

Rule 06.3 No text on screen sets below 13 px.

The smallest text on screen is 13 px, or 0.8125 rem: labels, tags and data labels. A label in capitals at 13 px takes Inter 700 with 6 percent tracking. A specimen that shows a mark or a minimum size at true size is a graphic, and its caption says so.

Tokens

  • --oa-type-labelInter 700, 0.8125rem/1.4
  • --oa-type-data-labelInter 600, 0.8125rem/1.3
  • --oa-type-captionInter 400, 0.875rem/1.5

Why it works

Basis Design judgment; Master Brief section 8, tension 1; decision T-9

Our fifth edition set its labels at 10 to 12 px, and its text census counted 833 of 2,346 rendered text elements under 13 px. A floor with no screen exceptions keeps eyebrows, tags and navigation readable without zoom. At 13 px, capitals need less tracking than they did at 10 px, so 6 percent keeps them open without pulling a word apart.

For builders

The shared check fails any text under 12.95 px, with SVG text measured at its rendered scale. A chart drawn in SVG has to keep its labels at 13 px on a phone, so draw a phone version rather than shrinking the desktop one.

Rule 06.4 Tracking tightens only as headings grow.

Tracking is the space added to or taken from every pair of letters. Display styles take negative tracking that eases as the size drops: −4.5 percent for titles, −4 percent for sections, −3 percent for H3 and −2 percent for H4. Reading styles keep the font’s own spacing, and labels in capitals open to +6 percent.

Tokens

  • --oa-type-titleInter Tight 800, 6.875rem/0.95
  • --oa-type-sectionInter Tight 800, 5rem/1.03
  • --oa-type-h3Inter Tight 800, 2rem/1.08
  • --oa-type-h4Inter Tight 800, 1.5rem/1.15
  • --oa-type-labelInter 700, 0.8125rem/1.4

Why it works

Basis Design judgment; our audit of the fifth edition, October 2026

Large type looks loose at the font’s own spacing, and small type looks cramped when it is pulled tight. Our fifth edition used −4.5 percent at every heading size from 24 to 110 px. Measured at 24 px in Inter Tight 800, that shrinks a word space from 4.5 px to 3.4 px, a cut of 24 percent, while the letters close up too.

For builders

Tracking lives in each style’s letter-spacing property, in em, so it scales with the size: letter-spacing: var(--oa-type-h3-letter-spacing). Never track body text.

Rule 06.5 Figures line up in tables, and negatives take the true minus sign.

Tables, trackers, scorecards and chart labels set tabular figures, which give every digit the same width so a column lines up. A negative number takes the minus sign (−, U+2212), never a hyphen, and the numbers in one column carry the same number of decimals.

Tokens

  • --oa-type-data-labelInter 600, 0.8125rem/1.3
  • --oa-type-figureInter Tight 800, 6.5rem/1
  • --oa-type-body-smallInter 400, 0.9375rem/1.6

Why it works

Basis Design judgment; chapter 02, house rule H07

A reader compares a column by its right edge, and proportional figures move that edge digit by digit. The hyphen is shorter than the minus and sits lower, so a hyphen before 245 can read as a dash. Chapter 02’s house rule H07 asks for the true minus in prose as well.

Specifications

Figures in tables and charts
Tabular, font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums
--oa-type-data-label
Big figures
Inter Tight 800, tabular
--oa-type-figure
Minus sign
− (U+2212); plus sign + (U+002B) where a sign is printed
Ligatures
Common on, discretionary off

For builders

In a template, write the minus as &amp;minus; or \2212. A chart script should format negatives itself, since a number converted to text takes a hyphen.

Rule 06.6 Headings balance their lines and never end on one word.

A heading that runs to two or more lines splits into lines of near equal length, and its last line holds at least two words. Body text wraps so its last line never holds one short word.

Tokens

  • --oa-type-h3Inter Tight 800, 2rem/1.08
  • --oa-type-sectionInter Tight 800, 5rem/1.03

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A lone word on a heading’s last line, called a widow, reads as an afterthought and pulls the eye down a line for one word. Balanced lines let a reader take in a heading at a glance.

Specifications

Headings
text-wrap: balance
--oa-type-h3
Body text
text-wrap: pretty
--oa-type-body

Related chapters

  • 02 Voice
  • 07 Layout and spacing

For builders

Older browsers ignore text-wrap and wrap as usual, so check the longest real heading at 360 px and, where a widow appears, join its last two words with a no-break space.

Rule 06.7 Opening quotation marks hang outside the text edge.

In a pull quote or a quote card, the opening mark sits in the margin, so the first letter of every line starts on the same edge. Use curly quotation marks and apostrophes, never straight ones, and keep common ligatures on and discretionary ligatures off.

Tokens

  • --oa-type-quoteLora 400, 2rem/1.3

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

When the mark sits inside the edge, the first line starts a mark’s width to the right of the rest, and the block looks indented by accident. Straight marks come from the typewriter; curly marks are the ones readers know from print.

Specifications

Hang
0.39 em in Lora Italic 400, measured
--oa-type-quote
Marks
“ ” ‘ ’ (U+201C, U+201D, U+2018, U+2019)

For builders

Set hanging-punctuation: first where the browser supports it, and a negative text-indent of 0.39 em on the quote where it does not.

Rule 06.8 Body text runs 60 to 75 characters a line.

Set body text to a measure of 60 to 75 characters a line on wider screens, and intro text to 65 at most. A phone gives about 38 to 40 characters, which suits a small screen. Chapter 07 gives the column spans that deliver these measures at each width.

Tokens

  • --oa-layout-measure-body-ideal33.88rem
  • --oa-layout-measure-body-max37.37rem
  • --oa-layout-measure-intro-max41.91rem
  • --oa-type-bodyInter 400, 1.0625rem/1.6
  • --oa-type-introInter 400, 1.375rem/1.5

Why it works

Basis Design judgment, with WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.8 (AAA, advisory)

Lines far past 75 characters make the eye lose its place on the way back to the next one. The ch unit, the width of a zero, runs wider than Inter’s average letter, so an intro set to 65ch, as in our fifth edition, measured 83 to 89 characters a line when we set it at 22 px.

Rule 06.9 Email sets its type in the system stack.

Many mail apps ignore web fonts, so email sets headlines and body text in Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, and quotations in Georgia Italic. The scale’s sizes and weights still apply, and chapter 22 shows the full template.

Tokens

  • --oa-font-family-email-sansHelvetica, Arial, sans-serif
  • --oa-font-family-email-quoteGeorgia, serif

Why it works

Basis Design judgment; Master Brief section 10

A mail app that cannot load a web font falls back to a face of its own choosing, often a serif. The system stack names the fallback in advance, so every reader sees a face we chose. Our fifth edition kept this rule and then set its own email headline in Inter Tight.

Specifications

Headlines and body
Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
--oa-font-family-email-sans

For builders

Write the stack on every text element of an email, inline, since many mail apps strip a style block. The wordmark goes in as an image with its name as alt text.

Rule 06.10 Pages load the three faces and never substitute another.

Pages load Inter Tight, Inter and Lora from their published files, in the weights the scale uses. Arial and Georgia appear only as fallbacks inside the font stacks. No other face stands in for ours, including Spectral, Source Sans, Public Sans, IBM Plex, Libre Baskerville, Playfair Display, Cormorant, Helvetica Neue for display, Times New Roman, Calibri, Roboto, Open Sans and Montserrat.

Tokens

  • --oa-font-family-display"Inter Tight", Arial, sans-serif
  • --oa-font-family-readingInter, Arial, sans-serif
  • --oa-font-family-quoteLora, Georgia, serif

Why it works

Basis Master Brief section 3; design judgment

Master Brief section 3 says a font substitution is never a finished identity decision. A fallback keeps a page readable when a font fails to load, and that is its only job. Measured at 32 px, the heading here sets 479 px wide in Inter Tight and 485 px in Arial, 1.3 percent wider, which is why a page that failed to load Inter Tight can look finished: only the letters show it. The list carries our fifth edition’s never-substitute list forward.

Foundations · Chapter 07 of 28

07 Layout and spacing

Build each page on the column grid and spacing scale, readable at every width.

Every page sits on a column grid and spaces its parts in steps of 8 px. The grid changes with the screen, from 12 columns on a desktop to four on a phone, and each paragraph spans the columns that keep its lines at the measure chapter 06 sets.

A page also has to read at 320 px wide, and with its text at twice the size, with nothing cut off and no scrolling sideways.

In this chapter

  • Rule 07.1 Space comes in steps of the 8 px scale.
  • Rule 07.2 Each page sits on the column grid for its width.
  • Rule 07.3 Body text spans the columns that hold its measure.
  • Rule 07.4 A heading sits closer to the text it introduces than to the block above.
  • Rule 07.5 Breakpoints are set in em, so larger text gets a narrower layout.
  • Rule 07.6 Every page reads at 320 px wide, with nothing lost.
  • Specifications
  • Related chapters
  • For builders

Rule 07.1 Space comes in steps of the 8 px scale.

Use the eleven steps of the spacing scale, from 4 px to 104 px, for every gap, padding and margin. Spaces around text are set in rem, so they grow with the reader’s text, and the grid’s gutters and page margins are set in px.

Tokens

  • --oa-space-1000.5rem
  • --oa-space-1500.75rem
  • --oa-space-2001rem
  • --oa-space-3001.5rem
  • --oa-space-4002rem
  • --oa-space-5002.5rem
  • --oa-space-6003rem
  • --oa-space-8004rem
  • --oa-space-10005rem
  • --oa-space-13006.5rem

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

One rhythm lets the parts of different pages line up, and a reader senses the order before reading it. Every step is a multiple of 4 px, so its edges land on whole device pixels at 1x, 1.5x, 2x and 3x screen density. Our fifth edition kept the same 8 px rhythm; Edition 06 gives each step a token.

Rule 07.2 Each page sits on the column grid for its width.

Lay each page on the grid for its width: 12 columns at 1440 and 1024 px, eight at 768 px and four on phones, with the gutters and margins in the specifications. Every section of a page shares the same column lines.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment; our audit of the fifth edition, October 2026

When every section uses the same column lines, the eye finds the edge of each block in the same place, page after page. Our fifth edition switched among two- to six-column grids from section to section, so no column line ran the length of a chapter.

Rule 07.3 Body text spans the columns that hold its measure.

Body text spans five of 12 columns at 1440 px, seven of 12 at 1024 px, six of eight at 768 px and all four on phones. Those spans hold the 60 to 75 characters a line that chapter 06 sets, and a block that spans more columns caps its text at the body measure.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

The grid places a block, and its span keeps the lines readable. A paragraph run across all 12 columns at 1440 px measured 165 characters a line, more than twice the measure, while the five-column span measured 66.

Rule 07.4 A heading sits closer to the text it introduces than to the block above.

Leave at least twice as much space above a heading as below it. Sections part by 80 px, a label sits 32 px below the block above it and 8 px above what it names, and paragraphs part by 16 px.

Tokens

  • --oa-space-10005rem
  • --oa-space-6003rem
  • --oa-space-4002rem
  • --oa-space-2001rem
  • --oa-space-1000.5rem

Why it works

Basis Design judgment, from the Gestalt principle of proximity

Readers group what sits close together, a pattern designers call proximity. A heading with equal space above and below seems to belong to neither block, and the reader pauses to work out which one it names.

Rule 07.5 Breakpoints are set in em, so larger text gets a narrower layout.

Write media queries in em, which follows the reader’s text size: 90em for the wide layout, 64em for desktop and 48em for tablet, with the phone layout as the base. On a 1440 px screen, a reader at 150 percent text gets the tablet layout and a reader at 200 percent the phone layout, with fewer, wider columns for the larger words.

Tokens

  • --oa-layout-breakpoint-wide1440px
  • --oa-layout-breakpoint-desktop1024px
  • --oa-layout-breakpoint-tablet768px

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.4

WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.4 Resize Text asks that text reach 200 percent with nothing lost. A breakpoint in px ignores the reader’s text size, so doubled text crowds a layout drawn for smaller words: five columns at 1440 px hold about 28 characters of 34 px text a line. In em, the layout steps down as the text grows, and the measure cap in rem keeps the line length.

--oa-layout-breakpoint-desktop

--oa-layout-breakpoint-tablet
Phone
The base layout, no query
--oa-layout-breakpoint-phone

For builders

Media queries cannot read custom properties, so write the em value itself: @media (min-width: 64em). The token’s mediaQuery field in tokens.json holds each one.

Rule 07.6 Every page reads at 320 px wide, with nothing lost.

At 320 CSS px, the width of a small phone or a desktop window zoomed to 400 percent, a page shows all its content without scrolling sideways. Tables stack into one card per row. Only content that needs two dimensions, such as a wide data table or a specimen at true size, scrolls inside its own labeled frame.

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10

WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.10 Reflow asks for content at 320 CSS px with no loss of information and no scrolling in two directions. When we tested our fifth edition at 320 px, the page ran 524 px wide and its contrast table lost its last column.

Foundations · Chapter 08 of 28

08 The Signal Grid

Keep the lockmark to its fixed places, and put a key beside every Signal Grid that codes content.

Democracy has a structure. The lockmark draws it as nine nodes joined by links, with the lever, a larger red node at bottom right, at the place where one change moves the rest. It sits beside the wordmark in the masthead and in a few fixed places, and its drawing never changes.

The Signal Grid uses the same nine nodes to code one thing about a piece: how far a bill has moved, which recurring series it belongs to, or which pillar it serves. A coded grid always sits beside words that say what it shows.

In this chapter

  • Rule 08.1 Draw the lockmark from its master for its size, and keep its drawing fixed.
  • Rule 08.2 Place the lockmark only in its fixed positions and sizes.
  • Rule 08.3 Set a key beside every Signal Grid that codes content.
  • Rule 08.4 Let each grid code one thing, chosen in this order: tracker progress, a series route, a pillar corner.
  • Rule 08.5 Show tracker progress with a shape for each stage, from 40 px.
  • Rule 08.6 Give each recurring series one fixed route that ends on its pillar’s corner.
  • Rule 08.7 Light one corner to name a pillar, and print the pillar’s name beside it.
  • Rule 08.8 Build the kicker from a 24 px grid, a 24 px icon and a label.
  • Rule 08.9 Keep every grid state still, and say it in words.
  • Specifications
  • Related chapters
  • For builders

Rule 08.1 Draw the lockmark from its master for its size, and keep its drawing fixed.

The lockmark is a 3 by 3 grid of nodes joined around its edge and through its center, with the lever in signature red at bottom right. Place the 16 px master from 16 to 23 px, the 24 px master from 24 to 47 px and Edition 05’s master from 48 px.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-identity-signature-on-newsprint#E63946
  • --oa-color-palette-stone#5D636D

Why it works

Basis Design judgment, measured in Chromium (Identity masters notes, October 28, 2026)

At small sizes Edition 05’s single master lost its shape: at 24 px only 5 percent of its ink was solid, and at 16 px the lever became one pink pixel. The small masters set every node and link on whole pixels and draw the lever one size up, so it still reads as the place where one change moves the rest.

Rule 08.2 Place the lockmark only in its fixed positions and sizes.

The lockmark appears in four places, once per view: at the bottom right of social cards, covers and posters, 40 px or 0.4 in, inside the margin; beside the wordmark in L3 and L6; beside the section label on report and slide pages, 24 px or 0.25 in; and in a chart legend at 16 px, where chapter 14 calls for it.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A signature works by turning up in the same place, so a reader finds it without looking. Used as a bullet or scattered as decoration, it stops signing the page.

Rule 08.3 Set a key beside every Signal Grid that codes content.

A coded grid sits beside words that say what it shows, on the same line or directly under it, at 13 px or larger: the stage and its name for a tracker, the series name for a route, the pillar’s name for a corner. Screen readers get the same words.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-text-secondary-on-newsprint#4E535B

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 1.1.1 and 1.4.1; Design judgment

Nine dots at 24 or 40 px cannot explain themselves, and Edition 05’s grids coded six things with no words nearby. With the words beside it, the grid becomes a shortcut for readers who know it and hides nothing from readers who do not.

Specifications

Key

For builders

Write the key from the record’s data, so the words and the grid can never disagree, and mark the grid aria-hidden="true" when the key sits beside it.

Rule 08.4 Let each grid code one thing, chosen in this order: tracker progress, a series route, a pillar corner.

When a piece could carry more than one code, its grid shows the first that applies. Progress may add the stage where a reader can take part now, and a series route always ends on its pillar’s corner. Content type is never coded by color; name it in words in the kicker.

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1; Design judgment

Edition 05’s grid coded pillar, content type, progress, gaps and series on the same nine nodes, and a reader could not tell which one was in front of them. Its four content-type colors look alike in grayscale, and its Verdigris and red differ at 1.14 to 1. One code per grid, chosen in a fixed order, gives every grid one meaning.

Rule 08.5 Show tracker progress with a shape for each stage, from 40 px.

A tracker grid reads its nine stages left to right and top to bottom. A filled disc marks a stage done; a ring marks the stage under way; a gap, with the node and its links cut away, marks a stage that never happened; a small Stone node marks a stage not yet reached. One red disc may mark the stage where a reader can take part now.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-palette-pillar-red#E63946
  • --oa-color-border-strong-on-newsprint#121212

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1; D1-21

Shapes survive grayscale, color blindness and a cheap printer. Edition 05 told the stage under way from a finished one by color alone, Verdigris against red at 1.14 to 1, and drew a missed stage as a dashed ring, a texture the atlas gives to a plausible link.

For builders

Give the red disc to the stage only while the reader can act, and only when no error holds the view’s red (Rule 05.3).

Rule 08.6 Give each recurring series one fixed route that ends on its pillar’s corner.

A series route runs along the links, never across a diagonal, and ends on the corner of the pillar the series serves. Six series hold six routes, and a new series takes a route no other series uses.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-graphic-essential-on-newsprint#121212

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A route lets a regular reader spot a series at a glance, and ending on the pillar’s corner ties each series to the pillar order: Explain top left, Track top right, Connect bottom left, Act bottom right.

Rule 08.7 Light one corner to name a pillar, and print the pillar’s name beside it.

The four corners follow the pillar order in reading order: Explain top left, Track top right, Connect bottom left, Act bottom right. Light one corner as a 7 px disc at 24 px, keep the other nodes small and Stone, and set the pillar’s name beside the grid.

Why it works

Basis R9 (DR-67); Design judgment

The pillars run Explain, Track, Connect, Act, and the corners take them in the order a page is read. Under 48 px a pillar mark sits with its word (R9), and the corner follows the same rule.

Rule 08.8 Build the kicker from a 24 px grid, a 24 px icon and a label.

The kicker, the short line above a title, sets the grid at 24 px, 12 px of space, a Civic Line topic icon at 24 px in one color, 12 px, then the series and the topic in the label style at 13 px. A record’s ID, when there is one, follows as a typed chip.

One definition keeps every kicker the same height and order on the site, in email and in reports. Edition 05 defined it twice, with 20 to 24 px grids and labels at 10 and 11 px, under the 13 px floor.

Rule 08.9 Keep every grid state still, and say it in words.

Empty, loading, ready, under way and final each have their own drawing and a line of text. Nothing pulses: loading shows the links alone, with the words “Loading tracker” in a status region that screen readers announce.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-state-loading-text-on-newsprint#4E535B
  • --oa-color-state-empty-text-on-newsprint#4E535B

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.2, 1.4.11 and 4.1.3

Edition 05 pulsed the lever between 20 and 50 percent opacity with no end and no pause, at 1.27 to 1.83 to 1 on Newsprint. That fails WCAG’s rules on moving content and on contrast for graphics, and the pulse told a reader nothing a word could not.

Specifications

Empty
Small nodes and links; “Nothing filed yet”
Loading
Links alone; “Loading tracker” in a status region
--oa-color-state-loading-text-on-newsprint
Ready
Stages done as filled discs; the stage in words
Under way
A ring on the current stage
Final
All nine filled
Motion
None; chapter 17 covers any change between states

Appendix · After chapter 08

Proofs for Gate 2

Compare each piece at both wordmark widths, side by side at actual size, before you choose at Gate 2.

Gate 2 settles the wordmark’s width and ampersand B as refined (DR-71). Each piece below appears twice at actual size, first at today’s width and then at the condensed width, both carrying ampersand B. Today’s width stays in force until you choose.

The studio recommends today’s width and B as refined (D2-30). At the same height the condensed drawing only runs narrower, and its heavy capitals sit close to the lettering of campaign signs. Its monogram also reads as 0&A.

The marks at a glance

The wordmark from each of its masters, the stacked lockup and the monogram, at the same height in both widths.

Masthead on the site

L3 in the 1440 px bar, with the phone bar under it. Both widths sit at the same height, so the condensed bar is shorter by 40 px.

Masthead in email

L3 at the head of a 600 px email. In a sent email it is a PNG at twice size with the alt text Oath & Action.

Avatar

The monogram, L8, on the Charcoal tile that R13 sets as the default, in a circle and a square. Feeds draw an avatar at about 32 to 48 px, where L8 at either width sets its capitals under the 14 px floor; ampersand B alone reads there and is the same at both widths, so the studio recommends B for avatars whichever width you choose.

Social card

The 1200 by 630 link-preview card, with a hinge headline whose ampersand takes the card’s working red. No web address until the site is settled (DR-55).

Letterhead

US Letter, 8.5 by 11 inches, at true size on screen (96 px to the inch). The print proof holds both widths, one per page; check its scale with a ruler before you judge it on paper.
